extracted.intended_audience: science bloggers, research-integrity journalists, and the broader research community interested in misconduct reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and informal standards for bloggers and journalists reporting alleged research misconduct, handling legal threats, and expectations for institutional investigations and retraction practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report only facts in the public domain
rubrics_metrics.description: “Retraction Watch is written very carefully and covers only facts in the public domain.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only verifiable, public-domain facts when writing about alleged misconduct to avoid defamation risk; avoid publishing unverified allegations or private information.

rubrics_metrics.name: When threatened legally, request specific allegations before acting
rubrics_metrics.description: From the post: “We called the law firm today to ask what statements in particular the letter referred to, and they said they would get back to us. We will respond appropriately once we hear the specific allegations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a lawyer demands removal or alleges defamation, ask for precise identification of the contested statements and details of the claim before deciding whether to retract or remove content.

rubrics_metrics.name: State reasons for retraction/correction publicly
rubrics_metrics.description: Noted practice/problem: some items were withdrawn/retracted/corrected mainly for problems with the images; in a couple of cases the reason for the removal was unstated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice for journals/institutions: when articles are withdrawn/retracted/corrected, give explicit reasons so the record is clear; unstated removals are poor practice and reduce transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional investigations: inform relevant parties and preserve due process/confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: “Generally their rules include due process, and require at least informing people. Ideally, when credible complaints are lodged, schools should quickly inform *all* those relevant, do inquiry/investigation expeditiously and confidentially...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should notify affected individuals, follow due process, conduct inquiries promptly, and maintain confidentiality during investigations to protect rights and integrity of the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional investigations: publish results and be clear about culpability
rubrics_metrics.description: “…and then publish results in both directions. I.e., if complaints are judged valid, they should say so, and if not (especially if complaints already public), should also say so explicitly, and in cases of multiple authorships, should be as clear as possible about which people if any were deemed at fault, and which were not.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After conclusion, institutions should publicly report outcomes clearly—affirming findings when misconduct is established and exonerating where appropriate; specify which coauthors (if any) were found responsible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency/open debate as remedy for poor science
rubrics_metrics.description: “The best disinfectant remains bright sunlight. Free and open debate remains the only way to test ideas.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage open discussion and public scrutiny of published work as a mechanism to detect and correct shoddy research; secrecy undermines trust and correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public record of retractions (indexing and accessibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment: “Also note that the retractions are a matter of public record, including indexing on PubMed (and presumably Google).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retractions and corrections should be clearly recorded in public indexes (e.g., PubMed) so readers and downstream users are informed of the corrected status of the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider legal protections such as anti‑SLAPP in response to strategic threats
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment: “California has an ‘anti-SLAPP’ statute that may apply... provides for attorneys fees, costs and punies if someone tries to SLAPP you.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When facing lawsuits aimed at chilling speech (SLAPPs), consider jurisdictional anti‑SLAPP statutes and seek legal advice; such protections may deter meritless suits and allow recovery of fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek pro bono or specialist legal help for threatened bloggers/journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment and offer from Popehat: connecting threatened bloggers with pro bono representation and investigating to write about bogus legal threats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bloggers and small outlets facing legal threats should consider contacting experienced free-speech or media-defense attorneys (pro bono if available) and specialist commentators who can assist publicly and legally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance privacy claims against public interest when research is public
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentary: a professor with many public papers, lectures, and public salary claiming privacy over research troubles raises questions about the limits of privacy for public-facing scientists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating privacy complaints about public researchers, weigh the individual's public disclosures and the public interest in scrutinizing publicly-funded or widely disseminated research; public professional activities reduce reasonable privacy expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attacking critics; focus on transparent corrective action
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple commenters: responses that counsel against using legal pressure to silence criticism and encourage addressing problems openly rather than suing critics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions and researchers should prioritize transparent correction and engagement rather than litigation aimed at suppressing critique, which can appear as 'thin‑skinned legal bullying' and damage reputations further.
